'''Beverly Jacques Anderson''' (born September 10, 1943) is an American [[mathematician]] and [[emeritus]] professor at the [[University of the District of Columbia]]. In the 1990s she worked at the [[National Academy of Sciences]] as Director of Minority Programs for the Mathematical Sciences Education Board, and led the ''Making Mathematics Work for Minorities'' program.

== Early life and education ==
Anderson grew up in the [[7th Ward of New Orleans|7th Ward]] of [[New Orleans]] in a time of [[Segregated school|segregation]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://awm-math.org/resources/careers/careers-that-count/|title=Careers That Count|website=Association for Women in Mathematics (AWM)|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-23}}</ref> She was born to Alvin Joseph and Dorothy Ann, who never finished high school.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iuniverse.com/bookstore/bookdetail.aspx?bookid=SKU-000185132|title=Cherished Memories|website=www.iuniverse.com|access-date=2019-03-23}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2006/08/30/sturdy-house-of-cards-span-classbankheadthe-jacques-sisters-of-new-orleans-play-the-hand-that-life-dealt-themspan/116811b6-6c8a-4278-a0ef-719aab269973/|title=Sturdy House of Cards The Jacques Sisters of New Orleans Play the Hand That Life Dealt Them|date=2006-08-30|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=2019-03-23}}</ref> Anderson attended [[Valena C. Jones School]], an elementary school.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orfila |first=Rebecca |date=August 2016 |title=Shared History - Valena Cecilia McArthur Jones |url=http://www.bslshoofly.com/1/post/2016/07/shared-history-august-2016.html |access-date=2019-03-23 |website=The Shoofly Magazine |language=en}}</ref> She attended a high school for African-Americans, where she excelled in mathematics.<ref name=":0" /> She earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics at [[Dillard University]]. She was the first member of her family to leave [[New Orleans]] when she moved to [[Howard University]] for graduate school.<ref name=":1" /> She completed a PhD at the [[Catholic University of America]] in 1978.<ref>{{cite thesis |title=Facilitating the Learning of General Abstract Denotative Concepts in Mathematics |date=1978 |publisher=Catholic University of America |type=PhD |id={{ProQuest|302914059}} }}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Anderson began teaching mathematics at the [[University of the District of Columbia]] in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/beverly-anderson-6761a427/|title=Dr. Anderson's LinkedIn page|last=LinkedIn|website=LinkedIn|language=en|access-date=2020-10-01}}</ref> She was awarded one of the faculty awards from the White House Initiative for Historically Black Colleges and Universities.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1988/11/10/cancer-society-award/65b8db00-4c65-4079-963d-5dcb5fc22dfe/|title=Cancer Society Award|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=2019-03-23}}</ref> She took a leave of absence to join the National Research Council of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1988, where she launched the ''Making Mathematics Work for Minorities'' program''.''<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Anderson|first=Beverly J.|date=1990|title=Minorities and Mathematics: The New Frontier and Challenge of the Nineties|journal=The Journal of Negro Education|volume=59|issue=3|pages=260–272|doi=10.2307/2295562|jstor=2295562}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/pubs/focus/past_issues/FOCUS_10_4.pdf|title=Focus: MAA|website=MAA|access-date=23 March 2019}}</ref> The program had three aims: to attract national attention to the need for minority students in mathematics, to identify best practice in mathematics education for minority students and develop a national strategy and alliance to improve mathematics education.<ref name=":2" /> She ran a series of workshops around the country, sharing ideas about how to help minorities excel in mathematics.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fUMrAAAAYAAJ&q=beverly+anderson+mathematics&pg=PA24|title=Making Mathematics Work for Minorities: Proceedings of the Region I Workshop|date=1989|publisher=National Academies|isbn=978-0-309-31837-2 |language=en}}</ref> Anderson argued that teaching mathematics without acknowledging the cultural bias that favoured students aligned with European tradition could significantly disadvantage people of colour.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x4nHBQAAQBAJ&q=%22Beverly+Anderson%22+mathematics&pg=PA204|title=Multicultural Curriculum: New Directions for Social Theory, Practice, and Policy|last1=Mahalingam|first1=Ram|last2=McCarthy|first2=Cameron|date=2013-10-28|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781136052224|language=en}}</ref>

Anderson identified that minority students enrolled in two-year college programs were 20% less likely to earn a bachelor's degree than those who started in four-year programs.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/5551535|title=Community Colleges: Promises or Preclusions|last=Anderson|first=Beverly J.|date=1991|publisher=Distributed by ERIC Clearinghouse|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref> She emphasized that school mathematics programs needed to be maintained long-term, for magnet schools to support the teaching profession and for comprehensive four-year college programs.<ref>{{Cite book|title=What has been done and what more must be done to recruit minorities in teaching mathematics|author=Anderson, Beverly J.|date=1992|publisher=[publisher not identified]|oclc=43536970}}</ref>

In her 40-year career at the University of the District of Columbia, Anderson was a Professor of Mathematics, Mathematics Department Chair, and Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences. She was made Provost and Vice President of Academic Affairs in 1997;<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://patch.com/maryland/laurel/three-new-appointees-fill-out-prince-georges-school-board|title=Three New Appointees Fill Out Prince George's School Board|date=2013-06-18|website=Laurel, MD Patch|language=en|access-date=2019-03-23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/glenn/news/pressrel/1999/99_36.html|title=NASA - NASA GRC News Release 99-36|website=www.nasa.gov|language=en|access-date=2019-03-23|archive-date=2019-03-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190323220902/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/glenn/news/pressrel/1999/99_36.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> however her appointment as provost was rescinded in 1999 after it was deemed to have been made without a proper search.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1999/07/02/provost-removed-because-national-search-not-done/68ba9b0b-6ee9-4c72-b551-048753c51ad8/|newspaper=The Washington Post|title=Provost Removed Because National Search Not Done|first=Valerie|last=Strauss|date=July 2, 1999}}</ref> She remained as a consultant on the National Academy of Sciences mathematics education program, serving as a consultant for the Everybody Counts report in 2000.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/everybodycountsr0000unse|title=Read "Everybody Counts: A Report to the Nation on the Future of Mathematics Education" at NAP.edu|language=en|doi=10.17226/1199|year=1989|isbn=978-0-309-03977-2|url-access=registration}}</ref> In 2013 Anderson was appointed to the [[Prince George's County, Maryland|Prince George's County]] School Board.<ref name="auto"/>
